topline: Four stories today: Spain's transport minister quits over the Urda rail disaster weeks before a snap election, hackers keep sabotaging supermarket freezers across Europe, candidate countries push back on the EU's probation plan as the enlargement package lands, and Europe rehearses a post-war Ukraine force as Brussels hosts security-guarantee talks.

stories.title: Spain's transport minister Óscar Puente resigns over the Urda train crash that killed 69
stories.summary: Óscar Puente announced his resignation on 3 November before parliament's standing committee, a week after two high-speed trains collided near Urda on the Madrid–Seville line, killing 69 people. According to Puente, a signalling failure stopped several trains and Madrid controllers then cleared a Renfe train to proceed while an Iryo train stood on the track ahead. It was the second deadly crash on the line this year after January's Adamuz accident, which killed 46. Puente, who had earlier ruled out quitting, said no minister could stay on after two disasters of this scale; Pedro Sánchez praised his decision. The government announced reduced services, a 40 km/h limit after signal failures, doubled insurance payouts and faster rollout of the EU's ERTMS signalling system.
stories.why: The resignation lands less than four weeks before Spain's 29 November snap general election, with polls already showing the PP and Vox ahead. It also puts the delayed rollout of the EU-standard ERTMS rail-safety system at the centre of a national political crisis.

left.angle: Left-leaning Spanish outlets present the resignation as a surprise act of political responsibility and dignity, and devote space to the government's safety and compensation measures. They also report that partners such as the Frente Amplio welcomed the move, while commentary pieces acknowledge that public trust in the railways remains damaged.

outlets.name: elDiario.es
outlets.note: Contrasts Frente Amplio's thanks for Puente's 'dignity' with PP and Vox turning their fire on Sánchez.

outlets.name: elDiario.es
outlets.note: Opinion piece arguing the resignation does not by itself end the crisis of confidence in rail.

outlets.name: Público
outlets.note: Live coverage built around Puente's own framing of the exit as coherence and empathy with victims.

right.angle: Right-leaning outlets treat the exit as overdue and as the end of a long run of controversies, from Puente's combative style on social media to earlier rail chaos. They shift the focus to Sánchez's responsibility and to the electoral calculation behind the timing.

outlets.name: The Objective
outlets.note: Casts the resignation as the culmination of a months-long rail crisis and lists Puente's past gaffes.

outlets.name: COPE
outlets.note: ABC's director suggests the timing reflects Moncloa reading private polls on Urda's electoral damage.

stories.differ: The left frames the resignation as a principled gesture and stresses the remedies; the right frames it as late, electorally driven and insufficient, aiming at Sánchez rather than Puente.

stories.title: Hackers overheat supermarket freezers in a second wave of attacks across Europe
stories.summary: Overnight into 2 November, internet-connected refrigeration units in supermarkets in at least nine countries, including Belgium, Luxembourg, Ireland, Sweden, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands and Germany, were remotely switched to defrost or heated, in some cases reportedly to 50°C. Retailers including Delhaize, Carrefour, SuperValu, Coop and ICA reported spoiled stock; one German store owner put his losses above €360,000. The wave follows an October attack on hundreds of French supermarkets. No group has claimed responsibility; EU Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen called it a deliberate attempt to disrupt the food chain but said food security is not at risk, Belgian prosecutors opened a criminal case and Italy held emergency talks. Equipment maker Danfoss said some customers had not applied a security update issued after the French incidents.
stories.why: The attacks hit a basic piece of civilian infrastructure in many member states at once and test the EU's new cyber-resilience rules for connected devices. They also feed an ongoing debate about hybrid pressure on Europe, though no attribution has been made.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage keeps attribution open and leans towards the systemic explanation: exposed, unpatched connected devices and operators who failed to act after the French warning. Al Jazeera mentions Russian hybrid-war suspicions only as background, while taz does not raise Russia at all.

outlets.name: taz
outlets.note: Focuses on German losses, missed security updates and why fridges need to be online at all.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Explainer weighing motives, stressing weak passwords and old controllers; no actor named.

right.angle: Right-leaning coverage leads with the possibility of hybrid warfare, putting pro-Russian hacker groups and state actors such as Russia and Iran front and centre while noting nothing is confirmed. It also stresses how unsophisticated the intrusions were and that official warnings went unheeded.

outlets.name: Apollo News
outlets.note: Headlines the hybrid-war question and lists earlier pro-Russian attacks on cooling systems.

stories.differ: Left-leaning pieces treat this mainly as an IoT-security and corporate-negligence failure; the right-leaning piece foregrounds a geopolitical sabotage frame, while both admit the culprit is unknown.

stories.title: Candidate countries push back on 'probation' and farm curbs as the EU's enlargement package is unveiled
stories.summary: At a Euronews enlargement summit in Brussels on 3 November, the day before Commissioner Marta Kos presents the 2026 enlargement package, candidates questioned the terms on offer. Montenegro, aiming to join by 2028, said it did not want second-grade membership, a reference to the Commission's proposed 15-year probation in which new members could lose votes or funds for backsliding. Ukraine's prime minister rejected permanent limits on farm exports such as grain after accession, while Albania repeated its goal of closing talks by end-2027 and North Macedonia said Bulgaria was holding its bid hostage. Armenia said applying in 2027 or 2028 was realistic, whereas Georgia offered no route out of its stalled bid. Croatia's prime minister warned that France's coming elections could derail enlargement.
stories.why: The package sets the pace for the most serious EU expansion push in two decades, and the safeguards debate will decide what kind of membership newcomers get. Unanimity means a single sceptical capital can still stall the process.

left.angle: No fresh left-leaning take on the summit was found in this run. Earlier centre-left coverage framed the probation plan as a lesson from the Orbán years, a way to protect EU values while keeping enlargement moving, and relied mainly on Commission voices.

outlets.name: The Guardian (via AOL, earlier — 6 Oct)
outlets.note: Earlier coverage: presents the 15-year probation as a 'No more Viktor Orbán' safeguard.

right.angle: No fresh right-leaning take on the summit was found in this run. Earlier centre-right/right coverage in The Spectator backed enlargement as a strategic necessity but noted critics would see probation as a de facto second tier and tied the debate to Britain's own relationship with the EU.

outlets.name: The Spectator (earlier — 10 Oct)
outlets.note: Earlier coverage: urges momentum but flags that safeguards could amount to second-class status.

stories.differ: Both sides' earlier coverage accepts enlargement as strategic; the centre-left stresses rule-of-law protection, while the right-leaning piece dwells on whether the safeguards create unequal members.

stories.title: Europe rehearses a post-war Ukraine force as Brussels hosts security-guarantee talks with the US
stories.summary: Representatives of Ukraine, the US, France, Germany, the UK, NATO and the World Bank meet at the European Commission on 4 November to discuss security guarantees and reconstruction, ahead of US-mediated Ukraine–Russia talks in Abu Dhabi on 10–11 November. Separately, Britain announced that about 2,800 troops from 11 countries, including 1,100 French and 300 British soldiers, will hold 'Koalicja', the first exercise of the Multinational Force for Ukraine, in south-eastern Poland from 9 to 22 November. The force, created by the coalition of the willing, would deploy only after fighting ends and at Kyiv's request, and is separate from NATO with limited US involvement. Russia's foreign minister has rejected a temporary ceasefire, while Zelensky wants Article 5-style US guarantees approved by Congress.
stories.why: Europe is trying to show it can underwrite Ukraine's post-war security itself as Washington drives the peace track. What is agreed on guarantees will shape EU reconstruction spending and Europe's own defence posture.

left.angle: Left-leaning coverage of the peace track leads with the human toll of continuing Russian strikes, such as the bombing of an aid centre in Zaporizhzhia, and relays Kyiv's view that Moscow is not serious about de-escalation. The European force and the Brussels meeting barely feature.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Pairs the deadly strike on an aid hub with the announcement of new US-mediated talks.

right.angle: Right-leaning British coverage centres on the role of UK troops in the exercise and on preparing for an eventual peace. A full right-leaning analysis of the risks or of the Brussels talks was not found in this run.

outlets.name: GB News
outlets.note: Headline puts British troops at the front of the multinational wargame for peace (full text not reviewed).

stories.differ: The left-leaning take stresses Russian violence and doubts about Moscow's intentions; the right-leaning take puts British military readiness and national contribution first.
